title: Derivatives of Exponentials and the Number e
hook: The video opens by admitting a deliberate gap in prior lessons—exponential derivatives were left out—then immediately promises to reveal why e is the most important base, creating curiosity through incompleteness.

scenes.purpose: Frame the lesson as filling a known gap; raise the central question

on_screen.desc: Video series strip with prior episodes highlighted
Known formulas: d(x^n)/dx and d(sin x)/dx

scenes.transition: Series strip stays; formulas and speech bubble fade as e^x grows and floats toward teacher
scenes.narration_gist: We have derivative formulas for powers and trig, but exponentials like 2^x were deliberately left out until now.

scenes.purpose: Ground the abstract function 2^t in a concrete, continuous real-world metaphor

on_screen.desc: Grid of Pi creatures doubling each day

scenes.transition: Pi creature grid grows day by day; function label transforms from P(t) to M(t)
scenes.narration_gist: Treat 2^t as a continuously growing population mass that doubles every day, making tiny changes in time meaningful.

scenes.purpose: Show the naive 'derivative equals itself' observation and immediately complicate it

on_screen.desc: Rectangle highlighting new creatures added in one day
Brace labeled 'Rate of change over one full day'

scenes.transition: Growth fraction transforms to show dt in denominator; brace label changes to 'in a small time'
scenes.narration_gist: Growth over a full day equals the population size, which is tempting but only an approximation—the true derivative needs infinitesimally small dt.

scenes.purpose: Derive the key algebraic structure: separate the t-dependent and dt-dependent parts
scenes.transition: Multiplicative factor 2^t extracted to left; mystery constant term isolated in parentheses on right
scenes.narration_gist: The exponential property splits the expression so that the dt-dependent mystery factor is completely separate from t, implying the derivative is proportional to itself.

scenes.purpose: Make the mystery constant tangible through numerical exploration
scenes.transition: Numerical expression updates as dt decreases; constant stabilizes and gets highlighted in blue
scenes.narration_gist: Plugging smaller and smaller dt values into the calculator shows the mystery constant converges to ~0.6931, a fixed number independent of t.

scenes.purpose: Introduce e as the natural base where the proportionality constant equals exactly 1

on_screen.desc: Question: 'Is there a base where the constant = 1?'

scenes.transition: Pattern table fades; e^t graph appears in stage with tangent line annotation
scenes.narration_gist: Comparing constants across bases reveals a pattern, and the special base e ≈ 2.718 is defined as the one where the proportionality constant is exactly 1.

scenes.purpose: Show e^t as self-slope on a graph, making the abstract definition visually concrete

on_screen.desc: Graph of e^t with tangent line at example point
Slope label = e^t matching height label

scenes.transition: Tangent slides along curve; slope label and height label stay equal throughout
scenes.narration_gist: On the graph of e^t, the slope of the tangent at any point exactly equals the height at that point—a visually memorable definition.

scenes.purpose: Resolve the mystery constants using chain rule and natural log
scenes.transition: Equation rewrites in place; ln(2) label replaces mystery constant and gets highlighted
scenes.narration_gist: Writing 2^t as e^{ln(2)·t} and applying the chain rule shows the mystery constant is precisely ln(2)—the natural log answers the question 'e to the what equals 2?'

scenes.purpose: Generalize to all proportional-growth phenomena and cement the e^{ct} convention

on_screen.desc: ODE: dΔT/dt = -kΔT with cooling curve graph
dM/dt = rM for invested money, solution e^{rt}

scenes.transition: Real-world examples appear side by side; e^{ct} form is shown as the natural writing convention
scenes.narration_gist: Whenever a quantity's rate of change is proportional to itself, it takes the form e^{ct}, and c is exactly that proportionality constant—making e the natural language for all exponential growth.

lessons: Open by naming an explicit gap from prior content so viewers feel they are completing something unfinished.
Anchor abstract functions in a physical metaphor before touching any algebra, so the manipulation has motivational grounding.
Use a staged false-then-corrected claim (derivative equals itself) to make precision feel earned rather than imposed.
Isolate the part of an expression that 'does the interesting thing' visually—box or brace it—before explaining why it matters.
Let numerics do persuasion before algebra: show a calculator converging to a mystery constant so the viewer already believes it before the proof.
Pair every algebraic resolution with a visual restatement (the self-slope graph) so viewers have two independent mental hooks for the same idea.
End with side-by-side real-world applications in split zones to show the same structure recurring, transforming the lesson from a trick into a universal principle.
tags: e euler exponential growth natural log derivative compound
